items.note: Flowers and garlands were indispensable in worship, and contemporary records frequently mention grants for flower gardens attached to temples.
Innumerable temples were built in the period, Bhoja alone being credited with the construction of several.

Kalvan inscription of Yasovarman, a feudatory of Bhoja, records land with flower garden, 14 Baniya shops, oil mills and 14 drammas given to a temple to defray worship expenses such as Abhisheka and Naivedya.
Part of the charity flowing into temples was used to maintain schools and colleges and feeding houses.
Sudi inscription of Somesvara I (Saka 976, A.D. 1054) states that temple posts were assigned according to functions and places.
Gift of land was regarded as the most pious deed; grants were made particularly on sacred occasions such as Samkrantis.
Bhoja issued his Ujjain plate (A.D. 1021) in the dark fortnight of Magha and the Betma plates on Magha Sudi 5.

items.note: Alberuni says the association of dancing girls with temples was disliked by learned men, yet kings maintained devadasis for revenue despite the Brahmin priests' opposition.
Alberuni states there were sixteen castes: the four well-known ones, five semi-untouchables and seven untouchables.
Brahmana caste names derived from territories; Srimala, Meval and Udichya Brahmanas migrated from northern India, especially Rajputana and Malwa, between 1000 and 1300 A.D.
The Ujjain plate of Bhoja and other records show that lands granted to temples were not entirely exempt from taxation.
Ujjain plate of Bhoja (A.D. 1021) records a grant of the village Viranaka to a Brahmana who had come into Malwa.
During Bhoja's reign a Kshattriya named Memmaka is referred to as cultivating a field in the Gwalior area.
